opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. What really excites me is the idea that intelligence doesn't have to live inside one giant monolithic model. If you look at how humans actually solve hard problems, it's rarely one person thinking in isolation. It's people proposing ideas, critiquing each other, catching mistakes, and gradually converging on something better than any individual started with.

We explored this in our work on multi-agent debate. You take several instances of a language model, each gives an initial answer to a question, then they read each other's responses and revise over a few rounds. What we found was surprisingly powerful: the final answers were significantly more accurate on things like arithmetic and reasoning, and much more factual. Hallucinations tended to get filtered out, because if one model makes something up, the others usually don't make up the *same* thing. They disagree, and that disagreement becomes a signal. Facts the models are confident about tend to stay consistent across agents, while fabricated details get challenged and dropped.

More broadly, this connects to something I care about a lot, which is compositionality. Instead of training one enormous model to do everything, you can combine smaller models, each maybe specialized in vision, language, planning, or physics, and have them communicate or jointly optimize toward a solution. That gives you a system that can generalize to new combinations of tasks it never saw during training, because you're composing pieces rather than relying on one model having memorized every scenario.

There's also a practical appeal. It's a form of scaling at inference time. Rather than only scaling parameters and data, you can scale how much reasoning and verification happens when you actually solve a problem. And it's modular: you can swap agents in and out, add new expertise, and inspect the conversation to understand why the system reached a conclusion.

So to me, a society of agents is a promising path toward systems that are more reliable, more interpretable, and better at generalizing, much like how human societies end up being far smarter than any single member.

r001.rationale: The response compares AI agents to people collaborating in human society, but does not draw an analogy to the brain’s decentralized organization.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. What I find really compelling about it is that a single large model, no matter how big, has a kind of built-in limitation: it generates an answer in one pass, and whatever errors or biases are baked into that pass just come out. It has no natural way to step back and check itself. But when you have multiple agents, even fairly small ones, and you let them propose answers, critique each other, and revise, you get something that looks a lot like how people actually reason together. One agent might make an arithmetic mistake, another catches it, and through a few rounds of back and forth the group converges on something more accurate than any individual started with.

The thing that surprised me early on is that this works even when all the agents are copies of the same model. You'd think they'd just agree with each other, but because of the randomness in sampling, they take different paths, make different mistakes, and the debate process filters those out. So you're getting a real improvement in factuality and reasoning without any additional training, just by changing how you use the model at inference time.

The broader reason I find it interesting is that it reframes intelligence as something that can emerge from a system rather than something that has to live inside one monolithic model. Scaling has gotten us a long way, but it's expensive, and at some point you want to ask whether there are other axes to push on. Composition is one of those axes. If small, specialized, or even imperfect agents can be combined to solve problems none of them could solve alone, that's a very different and, I think, more flexible path toward capable AI systems. It also makes the behavior more interpretable, because you can actually read the conversation and see where the reasoning went right or wrong, instead of staring at a single opaque output.

r001.rationale: The response compares agent debate to people reasoning together and describes intelligence emerging from a system, but it does not analogize the agents to the brain’s decentralized organization.

astra-6.text:
What I find interesting is that intelligence doesn’t necessarily have to live in a single model. You could have a collection of smaller agents, each with different capabilities, that work together to solve a problem that none of them could solve individually. One agent might propose an idea, another might critique it, and another might test it.

But the key question is how to make that interaction useful. If all the agents think the same way and make the same mistakes, having more of them doesn’t necessarily help. You want them to contribute different information and be able to correct each other. So building that society becomes a question of both what each agent can do and how they communicate.

r001.rationale: The response describes smaller agents with different capabilities collaborating and correcting one another, but it does not compare their organization to the brain.

sol-6.1.text:
What I find interesting is that intelligence might emerge from the interaction between agents, rather than having to live inside a single model. You could have small agents that each have different capabilities or different perspectives, and let them communicate to solve a problem together.

For example, one agent might propose a solution, another might critique it, and a third might test it. The question is whether those interactions actually produce something more capable and reliable than any individual agent. Just having more agents talking doesn’t guarantee that—they could reinforce the same mistake. So understanding how to structure that communication, and when it helps, is a really interesting research problem.

r001.rationale: The response describes intelligence emerging through communication among agents, but it does not compare that society to the brain’s decentralized organization.
